cvEn:
Asaf Waksman, son of Rachel and Leon, was born on 17 Cheshvan 5740 (6 November 1979) in Holon. About three years later his sister, Efrat, joined the family. From the first moment, Asaf felt love for her, cared for her devotedly, and never once was jealous of her. This special bond lasted throughout his life.

Asaf was also a close friend to his parents, a loving, caring and supportive son, and he showered the members of his family with endless love. Asaf grew up in a very close-knit family that liked to spend their free time together in restaurants, on trips, over carefully prepared weekend meals, and simply over everyday conversation and television.

Asaf had many friends. His close friends said they envied him for his close and unusual relationship with his parents and his sister. Generous by nature toward those around him, Asaf touched the lives of many. He always spoke to everyone with warmth, and tried to interest them in books he loved, good music, or interesting foods. People loved him for his warm and sincere attitude, and for his boundless capacity to give. Asaf was a very honest and principled man who strove for justice and showed a rare consideration for others.

In his short life, Asaf managed to do so much that it is hard to describe where he would have gone had his life not been cut short. He began his studies at the Yigal Allon Elementary School in Holon, continued at "Kiryat Ganim" Middle School in Rishon LeZion, and completed them at the "Makif Heh" High School. He was an outstanding student, and at the age of seventeen he passed the psychometric exam with a score of 752 without needing a preparatory course.

In his military service, Asaf was a combat observer and was recommended for officer training. During his service he served as a deputy commander in a training unit and as a team sergeant at the "Hazaka" outpost.

After his discharge, Asaf travelled to the Far East with his childhood friend, Idan Ben-Ami. The two travelled for four months in India, Nepal and Thailand, and gathered many experiences. After returning to Israel, Asaf began studying at the Technion, in one of its most prestigious programs: computer and software engineering. Upon completing his studies he joined the company Orbotech as a computer engineer, and worked there for about a year and a half. As part of his role he travelled twice to South Korea and succeeded in his work with the client.

But above all, Asaf was a man of books, a true intellectual. His private collection included over a thousand books, all of them quality works by the great writers of the world, covering a very wide range of subjects: fiction, poetry, music, art, philosophy and more. For example, he read James Joyce's "Ulysses" in English, a book considered one of the most difficult ever written in that language, if not the most difficult. One of his dreams was to build a large library in his own home. Only on the last Friday before his death, Asaf bought seven books, among them "Diplomacy" by Henry Kissinger, "Poems" by E. E. Cummings, and "The Structure of Scientific Revolutions" by Thomas S. Kuhn. Asaf was a true renaissance man.

Other areas in which Asaf showed a special interest were music and cooking. In cooking he was very creative; he drew on cookbooks but took the recipes into other territories. His taste in food was refined and discerning, and he loved to pamper his family and friends with the dishes he prepared. In music he amassed a very large collection of CDs in all the genres he loved: classical music (especially Chopin), jazz, rock and more. How sad that his young life ended to the sound of gunshots by the firing squad at his funeral. Asaf, the man of spirit, the humane and principled man, was buried in a military plot with a military funeral.

In the reserves, Asaf served as a commander of an intelligence cell in the Yahmam battalion (Target Intelligence Unit).

Asaf's life was cut short on 2 Kislev 5768 (12 November 2007), during a company exercise conducted by his reserve battalion in the Golan Heights. The armored personnel carrier he was driving overturned, and Asaf was killed. The investigation of the accident revealed that the day before, Asaf had been required to serve as an APC driver due to a shortage of drivers. Asaf warned his company commander that he was not skilled at driving an APC, and that the last time he had driven one was nine years earlier, during a four-day course he had taken. Despite this, Asaf was not released from the task and was required to drive the APC over an extremely difficult route. The training accident was investigated by a military inquiry committee and by the military police investigators. The military prosecution ordered indictments against four of Asaf's commanders for causing death through negligence.

The family, feeling that the death was needless, still has to go on living. Since the day Asaf was killed, his parents feel that not only was his young and beautiful life cut short, but theirs as well, and that the loss is unbearable.

Like every young man, Asaf had many dreams. Professionally, he aspired to work in building computers. Personally, since he loved children, he planned to start a family. He of course wanted to travel to interesting places, especially London and New York, to go on book-buying trips, and to attend concerts by the artists he loved. But all his dreams were cruelly cut short. Asaf left behind a giant void that will never be filled.

Asaf was twenty-eight when he fell. He was laid to rest in the military cemetery in Rishon LeZion. He is survived by his parents and his sister.

His friend Yoni Kelpach delivered a eulogy: "To tell the truth, writing is not my strong suit, and yet, without any prior hesitation, I decided to write this letter, although I do not know you at all. What led me to write this letter to you is one person, one person named Asaf." I knew Asaf for a very short time, sometime this year during the last reserve service we had in the north of the country. I do not serve with him in the same platoon, but for various reasons I was attached to his platoon, Platoon 5. Platoon 5 is made up of a not-small number of soldiers, and all of them, without exception, are the finest sons living in this land. But without a doubt, at least in my view, one young man stood out: Asaf. "I do not intend to write a fiery speech, nor do I intend to use lofty expressions. I will just say this: Asaf was, and still is, a man who, beyond his impressive appearance in everyone's eyes, is a heart. One beautiful and big heart that radiates calm and love to everyone around him. Asaf is an unusually intelligent young man and, to an equal degree, remarkably modest. A man of listening and understanding, and that is what made me value him so much in the very short time we were together. So what remains to be said, coming from my heart, is that Asaf has indeed left, but he has not disappeared. Be strong."

Eliel Pressburger wrote: "I first met Asaf in the reserves, on the last line we manned guarding the northern border. When I first saw him, I discovered a pleasant and restrained man with clever eyes and a shy smile. As time passed, I discovered a man overflowing with goodness, a desire to help, always ready to offer a shoulder." "Asaf, when I came to visit and console at your home, they showed me many books on various and diverse subjects that you were interested in, including three books you had bought before the reserve service and had been reading simultaneously, with the bookmarks still where you had stopped. There was a book by Henry Kissinger, a book of poetry, and a book of nonfiction. Then it became clear to me how full and rich your world was, and I came to see how complex and sensitive you were, with rare depth." "An image of that line is engraved in my memory: when we returned to base and went to sleep after several days of strenuous and exhausting activity guarding the northern border, I looked at the friends in the room, all sleeping, and only you were still awake, bent over one of the books you had brought, trying to read a few more pages before falling asleep." "Asaf, you had a highly realistic outlook combined with philosophical thought and poetry. An analytical ability alongside a wonderful sensitivity. And above all of that, you were a person." "As time passes and I hear and gather more and more stories about you, I understand how great a man you were. You could choose from so many different areas of interest. You touched on diverse and even opposing worlds. You combined matter and spirit. Yet you always kept the people around you in mind: always ready to help, to listen, to show interest, to advise, all with graciousness and a smile, with such a good feeling that you gave to those around you, and without a trace of arrogance or disdain on your part." "Today, when I teach students, I always stress to them the importance of the saying of our Sages: 'Derech eretz preceded Torah,' and explain to them that no matter how brilliant a person is in music, science or anything else, if he does not know how to be in the presence of other people, he is not a complete person." "And for me, Asaf, above all else, you will remain a personal example of 'derech eretz,' of being in the purest and truest sense: a human being." "May your soul be bound up in the bond of life."
